The distances between the airports of a country are pairwise different. From each airport a plane takes off and lands at the closest airport. Prove that there is no airport at which the number of landed planes exceeds $5$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral satisfying $AC<BD<AD$ and $\angle DBA<90^\circ$. Let $E$ be the point of the line parallel to $(AB)$ through $D$ such that $AC=DE$ and such that the points $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of the line $(AD)$. Let $F$ be the point of the line parallel to $(CD)$ through $A$ such that $BD=AF$ and such that the points $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of the line $(AD)$.
Show that the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $[BC]$ and $[EF]$ meet on the circumcircle of the quadrilateral $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram and let $M$ be the intersection of the diagonals. The circumcircle of $\triangle ABM$ intersects the segment $AD$ in $E\ne A$ and the circumcircle of $\triangle EMD$ intersects the segment $BE$ in the point $F\ne E$.

Prove that $\angle ACB=\angle DCF$.

Two triangles are drawn in a plane. The side lengths of one of them are $a$, $b$ and $c$ decimetres. The angles of the other one are $a$, $b$ and $c$ radians. Winnie-the-Pooh looks at the triangles and thinks: since the side lengths of the first triangle equal the angles of the second one, these triangles are congruent. Strange as it is, he turned out to be right! Prove that both triangles are equilateral.
Determine the values $x,y$ for which the expression $$\frac{2-\left(\dfrac{x+y}{3}-1\right)^2}{\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}+\dfrac{2y-x}{3}\right)^2+4}$$ takes the maximum value.

Let $c\ge 2023$ be some real number. $2023$ boxes are given. Each of them contains balls (possibly not the same number of balls). For every ball there is a corresponding integer $k$ such that the weight of the ball equals $c^k$. The sum of the weights of the balls in each box is the same. Consider the set of the balls in all the boxes, and suppose that in this set the number of balls of any one weight does not exceed $b$. Find the smallest possible value of $b$.

(a) Prove that no function $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfies $\gcd(f(m)+n,f(n)+m)=1$ for all distinct positive integers $m,n$. (b) Prove that a function with $\gcd(f(m)+n,f(n)+m)\le2$ for all such pairs does exist.

Let $a, b, c$ be pairwise distinct real numbers. Prove that
$$\left(\frac{2a - b}{a - b}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2b - c}{b - c}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2c - a}{c - a}\right)^2 \ge 5.$$

Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of positive real numbers. Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that $$x(f(x) + f(y)) \geq (f(f(x)) + y)f(y)$$ for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$.

The infinite sequence
$$1,2,3,4,0,9,6,9,4,8,7,\ldots$$
contains only numbers belonging to the set $\{0,1,2,\ldots,9\}$ and is constructed as follows: after the fourth number, each new number is the units digit of the sum of the four preceding numbers.

(a) Do the numbers $2,0,0,5$ appear consecutively in this sequence?

(b) Do the numbers $1,2,3,4$ appear consecutively a second time in this sequence?

Consider a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for which there exist a differentiable function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of strictly positive real numbers converging to $0$ such that
$$g'(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(x + a_n) - f(x)}{a_n}$$
for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

a) Give an example of such a function $f$ which is not differentiable at any point $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

b) Prove that if $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, then $f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute angled triangle. Points $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the sides $AC$ and $AB$, respectively, such that $$BC^2 = BA \times BF + CE \times CA.$$ Prove that for all such $E$ and $F$, circumcircle of the triangle $AEF$ passes through a fixed point different from $A$.
Let $x$, $y$ be real numbers such that the three numbers $$x-y,\qquad x^2-y^2,\qquad x^3-y^3$$ are positive prime numbers. Prove that $x-y=3$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB=BC$, the circumcentre $O$ and incentre $V$ lie inside the triangle. Point $X$ on side $BC$ is chosen so that $VX$ is parallel to $AB$. Prove that $OX$ and $CV$ are perpendicular.

Let $\alpha, \beta$ be distinct real numbers. Define the sequence of real numbers $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ for $n \ge 1$ by $$A_n = \frac{\alpha^n - \beta^n}{\alpha - \beta}.$$ Show that if for some prime $p$ the terms $A_p, A_{p+1}, A_{p+2}$ are integers, then all terms of the sequence are integers.

A rectangular $20 \times 19$ piece of paper, divided into unit squares, is cut into several square pieces, the cuts being made along the sides of the unit squares. Such a square piece is called an odd square if the length of its side is an odd number.

a) What is the minimum possible number of odd squares?

b) What is the smallest value that the sum of the perimeters of the odd squares can take?

a. In the triangle $ABC$, $X$ lies on the side $BC$, $Y$ on the side $CA$, and $Z$ on the side $AB$ with $YX \parallel AB$, $ZY \parallel BC$ and $XZ \parallel CA$. Show that $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are the midpoints of the respective sides of $ABC$.

b. In the triangle $ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on the side $BC$, with $CE = BD$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AD$. Show that the centroid of $ABC$ lies on $ME$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with orthocentre $H$, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ denote the respective midpoints of line segments $AB$, $AC$, and $AH$. The reflections of $B$ and $C$ in $F$ are $P$ and $Q$, respectively.
(a) Show that lines $PE$ and $QD$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.
(b) Prove that lines $PD$ and $QE$ intersect on line segment $AH$.

A positive integer $n$ is given. $2n$ rooks were placed on a $2n \times 2n$ board so that no two of them stand in the same row or the same column. After that the board was cut along the grid lines into two connected parts symmetric to each other with respect to the centre of the board. What is the largest possible number of rooks in one of the parts? (A grid figure is called connected if from any of its cells one can reach any other cell within the figure, moving each time to a cell sharing a side.)

In a triangle $ABC$, the median $AD$ (with $D$ on $BC$) and the angle bisector $BE$ (with $E$ on $AC$) are perpendicular to each other. If $AD = 7$ and $BE = 9$, find the integer nearest to the area of triangle $ABC$.

We call a positive integer $q$ a convenient denominator for a real number $\alpha$ if $\left|\alpha - \frac{p}{q}\right| < \frac{1}{10q}$ for some integer $p$. Prove that if two irrational numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have the same set of convenient denominators then either $\alpha + \beta$ or $\alpha - \beta$ is an integer.

Define set $S_n=\{1,2,\cdots,n\}$. $X$ is a subset of $S_n$. We call sum of all numbers in $X$ capacity (capacity of empty set is $0$). If capacity of $X$ is odd/even, then we call it odd/even subset.(a) Prove that the number of odd subsets and even subsets of $S_n$ are the same.(b) Prove that the sum of capacity of all odd subsets and even subsets are the same when $n\geq3$.(c) Calculate the sum of capacity of all odd subsets when $n\geq3$.

Points $P$ and $Q$ inside a triangle $ABC$ with sides $a,b,c$ and angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ satisfy $\angle BPC=\angle CPA=\angle APB=120^\circ$ and $\angle BQC=60^\circ+\alpha$, $\angle CQA=60^\circ+\beta$, $\angle AQB=60^\circ+\gamma$. Prove that $$(AP+BP+CP)^3\cdot AQ\cdot BQ\cdot CQ=(abc)^2.$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, $D$ the midpoint of $BC$, $E$ a point on the segment $AC$ such that $BE=2AD$, and $F$ the point of intersection of $AD$ with $BE$. If the angle $DAC$ measures $60^\circ$, find the measures of the angles of the triangle $FEA$.

In a triangle $ABC$, points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are taken on the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ respectively, such that the areas of the triangles $AFE$, $BFD$ and $CDE$ are equal. Prove that
$$\frac{(DEF)}{(ABC)} \geq \frac{1}{4}.$$
Note: $(XYZ)$ is the area of triangle $XYZ$.

A subset $S$ of the integers is called Saxonian if for every three pairwise different elements $a,b,c\in S$ the number $ab+c$ is a perfect square. Prove that any Saxonian set is finite and determine the largest possible number of elements that a Saxonian set can have.

Let $ABC$ be equilateral and $P_0$ outside it, with $AP_0C$ an isosceles right triangle, right-angled at $P_0$. A grasshopper jumps from $P_0$ to its reflection $P_1$ about $A$, then to the reflection $P_2$ of $P_1$ about $B$, then to the reflection $P_3$ of $P_2$ about $C$, and repeats these reflections about $A,B,C$. Compare $P_0P_1$ and $P_0P_n$ for $n\in\mathbb N$.

A point $T_0$ on the parabola $\mathcal{P}$ with equation $y^2=2px$ is given, together with a point $T_0'$ such that the midpoint of the segment $\overline{T_0T_0'}$ lies on the axis of the parabola $\mathcal{P}$. For a variable point $T$ on $\mathcal{P}$, different from $T_0$ and from the point symmetric to $T_0$ with respect to the axis of the parabola, the perpendicular from the point $T_0'$ to the line $T_0T$ meets the line through $T$ parallel to the axis of the parabola at a point $T'$. What is the locus of the point $T'$?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $2012$ with real coefficients such that for all real numbers $a,b,c$ with $a+b+c=0$ $$P(a)^3+P(b)^3+P(c)^3\ge 3P(a)P(b)P(c).$$ Can the polynomial $P(x)$ have exactly $2012$ distinct real roots?

(a) Does there exist a matrix of size $2n\times(2n+1)$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$, whose entries are natural numbers and such that the sum of the entries in every row and every column is a prime number? (b) Does there exist a matrix of size $14\times 2003$ with the same property?
A line is drawn through the midpoint of one of the lateral sides of a trapezoid, dividing the trapezoid into two regions of equal area. Determine the line.

Call white the numbers of the form $\sqrt{a+b\sqrt2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are non-zero integers. Similarly, call black the numbers of the form $\sqrt{c+d\sqrt7}$, where $c$ and $d$ are non-zero integers. Can a black number be equal to a sum of several white ones?

We call a set $B$ of natural numbers loyal if there exist natural numbers $i\le j$ such that $B=\{i,i+1,\ldots,j\}$. Let $Q$ be the set of all loyal sets. For every subset $A=\{a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_k\}$ of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ set $$f(A)=\max_{1\le i \le k-1}(a_{i+1}-a_i)\qquad\text{and}\qquad g(A)=\max_{B\subseteq A,\ B\in Q} |B|,$$ and define $$F(n)=\sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,n\}} f(A)\qquad\text{and}\qquad G(n)=\sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,n\}} g(A).$$ Prove that there exists $m\in \mathbb N$ such that $F(n)>G(n)$ for every natural number $n>m$. (Here $|A|$ is the number of elements of $A$, and $f(A)=0$ if $|A|\le 1$.)

In the first week after Bill's birthday, his uncle gave him some money for his new piggy bank. Every week after that, Bill put £2 into his piggy bank.
By the end of the ninth week after his birthday, Bill had trebled the amount his uncle gave him. How much, in pounds, did Bill have in total at the end of the ninth week?

Messages are coded using sequences consisting of zeroes and ones only. Only sequences with at most two consecutive ones or zeroes are allowed. (For instance the sequence $011001$ is allowed, but $011101$ is not.) Determine the number of sequences consisting of exactly $12$ numbers.
Inside the triangle $ABC$ a point $P$ is chosen with $\angle BAP = \angle CAP$. If $|AB|\cdot |CP| = |AC|\cdot |BP| = |BC|\cdot |AP|$, find all possible values of the angle $\angle ABP$.
Find all pairs of positive integers $(x, y)$ such that $x^3 + 9x^2 - 11x - 11 = 2^y$.
Find all solutions of the equation $$p^m-n^3=27,$$ where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers and $p$ prime number.

A company of thirty people sits at a round table. Each of them is either a fool or a clever person. Everybody sitting at the table is asked: "Is your neighbour on the right clever or a fool?" In answer, a clever person tells the truth, while a fool may either tell the truth or lie. It is known that the number of fools does not exceed $F$. For what largest value of $F$ is it always possible, knowing these answers, to point out a clever person in this company?

find all $k$ distinct integers $a_1,a_2,...,a_k$ such that there exists an injective function $f$ from reals to themselves such that for each positive integer $n$ we have $$\{f^n(x)-x| x \in \mathbb{R} \}=\{a_1+n,a_2+n,...,a_k+n\}$$.

A positive integer $n$ is given. Auksė and Baltrus play the following game, making moves alternately. In a move a player must choose any of the numbers $1,2,3,4,5$ and write it on the board. Auksė makes the first move. The game ends when the two players have made $n$ moves in total. If the sum of the $n$ written numbers is divisible by $9$, Baltrus wins; otherwise Auksė wins. Determine all values of $n$ for which Auksė has a winning strategy.

Determine all functions $f:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$f(x)f(y)=f(xy)+\frac1x+\frac1y$$
for all positive real numbers $x,y$.

Let $a, b, c$ be positive reals. Prove that
$$\frac{(b+c-a)^2}{2a^2+(2a+b+c)^2}+\frac{(c+a-b)^2}{2b^2+(a+2b+c)^2}+\frac{(a+b-c)^2}{2c^2+(a+b+2c)^2}\ge\frac{1}{6}.$$
Prove that any two numbers of the sequence $$2^2+1,\ 2^{2^2}+1,\ \dots,\ 2^{2^n}+1,\ \dots$$ are relatively prime.

Prove that there exist infinitely many triples $(x,y,z)$ of positive integers such that
$$x^2+y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx=6xyz.$$

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral. $K$, $L$, $M$, $N$ are the midpoints of segments $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$. $H_1$, $H_2$, $H_3$, $H_4$ are the orthocenters of triangles $AKN$, $KBL$, $LCM$ and $MND$. Prove that $H_1H_2H_3H_4$ is a parallelogram.
Suppose we want to make a pyramid with a square base out of stone balls. If we need $n$ stone balls for a base line, then how many stone balls of the same size do we need to make the pyramid?

There are ten boxes containing nine numbers; the last box is empty. A number may be moved from its box into the empty box. This counts as one operation. After that, the box in which the number was has become empty. Initially the order of the numbers is $8,7,3,9,1,5,2,6,4$. What is the least number of operations needed to get the numbers in increasing order, with the empty box last again? Why can it not be done in fewer operations than that?

Two sisters have two-digit ages. When they are juxtaposed (written next to each other), the four-digit number obtained is a perfect square. In $23$ years they will still have two-digit ages which, juxtaposed in the same order, will again form a perfect square. What are the ages of these two sisters today?

Prove that for any natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ such that $\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{a_k}>1$, the equation $\left[\frac n{a_1}\right]+\left[\frac n{a_2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac n{a_k}\right]=n$ has at most $a_1a_2\ldots a_k$ solutions in natural numbers. ($[x]$ is the integer part of the number $x$, that is, the largest integer not exceeding $x$.)

In acute-angled triangle $ABC$, the altitude of $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$. Suppose that $X$ is a point such that $\angle AXB=\angle DXM=90^\circ$ (assume that $X$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of the line $BM$). Show that $\angle XMB=2\angle MBC$.

Let $n \ge 2$ be some fixed positive integer and suppose that $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are positive real numbers satisfying $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = 2^n - 1$.

Find the minimum possible value of $$\frac{a_1}{1} + \frac{a_2}{1 + a_1} + \frac{a_3}{1 + a_1 + a_2} + \cdots + \frac{a_n}{1 + a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_{n-1}}.$$
We want to cover completely the three faces meeting at one vertex of a cube with edge length $k$ using $k^2$ labels of size $3 \times 1$. For which $k$ can this be done?

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers with $ab + bc + ca = 3$. Show that
$$\frac{bc}{1 + a^4} + \frac{ca}{1 + b^4} + \frac{ab}{1 + c^4} \ge \frac{3}{2}.$$

We write '$pq$' to denote the two-digit integer with tens digit $p$ and units digit $q$.
For which values of $a$, $b$ and $c$ are the two fractions $\dfrac{\text{'}ab\text{'}}{\text{'}ba\text{'}}$ and $\dfrac{\text{'}bc\text{'}}{\text{'}cb\text{'}}$ equal and different from $1$?

Circle $I$ is the incircle of $\triangle ABC$. Circle $I$ is tangent to sides $BC$ and $AC$ at $M,N$ respectively. $E,F$ are midpoints of sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Lines $EF, BI$ intersect at $D$. Show that $M,N,D$ are collinear.

Every question of an exam was solved by exactly four students, and every pair of questions was solved by exactly one student. If no student solved all the questions, determine the maximum possible number of questions in this exam.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC \ne 45^\circ$ and $\angle ABC \ne 135^\circ$. Let $P$ be the point on the line $AB$ with $\angle CPB = 45^\circ$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcentres of the triangles $ACP$ and $BCP$. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral $CO_1PO_2$ is equal to the area of the triangle $ABC$.
Let $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be strictly decreasing. Find all possible real values of $x$ satisfying $f(3x^2+5x+1)<f(4x^2-5x-6)$.

A right triangle has legs of lengths $a$ and $b$. A circle of radius $r$ is tangent to both legs and has its centre on the hypotenuse of the right triangle. Prove that $$\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}=\frac{1}{r}.$$

In an acute triangle $ABC$, $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$ and $C$, respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, $S$ the midpoint of the segment $AH$, and $G$ the intersection of the segments $FE$ and $AH$. If $N$ is the intersection point of the median $AM$ and the circumcircle of triangle $BCH$, prove that $\angle HMA = \angle GNS$.
Positive real $x,y,z$ satisfy $xy+yz+zx=3xyz$. Prove that $x^2y+y^2z+z^2x\geq2(x+y+z)-3$. When does equality hold?
A prime number $p \ge 5$ is given. Write $$\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{4} + \dots + \frac{p-3}{p-1} = \frac{a}{b}$$ for natural numbers $a$ and $b$. Show that $p$ divides $a$.

The vertices of 2013-polygon are labelled by numbers (each vertex was labelled by exactly one number) such that the sum of numbers(labels) on any nine consecutive vertices is equal to 300. If vertex $A_{13}$ is labelled by a number 13, and vertex $A_{20}$ by a number 20, find the label of vertex $A_{2013}$.

In a country there are $2000$ cities, and the distances between any two cities are all distinct. It is known that among any three cities, the two cities whose distance is the smallest are not connected by a road. Find the maximum possible number of roads in this country.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle such that $AB < AC$. Let the excircle opposite to $A$ be tangent to the lines $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ at the points $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively, and let $J$ be its centre. Let $P$ be a point on the side $BC$. The circumcircles of triangles $BDP$ and $CEP$ intersect for the second time at $Q$. Let $R$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line $FJ$. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are collinear. (The excircle of triangle $ABC$ opposite to $A$ is the circle tangent to the segment $BC$, to the ray $AB$ beyond $B$ and to the ray $AC$ beyond $C$.)

Show that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that the equation $P(x)=0$ has no integer solutions, but for every positive integer $n$ there exists $x\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $n\mid P(x)$.

An equilateral triangle $\Delta$ of side length $L > 0$ is given. Suppose that $n$ equilateral triangles with side length $1$ and with non-overlapping interiors are drawn inside $\Delta$, such that each unit equilateral triangle has sides parallel to $\Delta$, but with opposite orientation. Prove that $$n \le \frac{2}{3} L^2.$$
Let $2^{-n_1}+2^{-n_2}+\cdots+2^{-n_k}+\cdots$, where $1\le n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_k<\cdots$, be the binary expansion of $(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$. Prove that $n_k\le 2^{k-1}-2$ for all integers $k\ge 4$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $AB = 1$, $\angle BAE = \angle ABC = 120^\circ$, $\angle CDE = 60^\circ$ and $\angle ADB = 30^\circ$. Prove that the area of the pentagon $ABCDE$ is less than $\sqrt{3}$.

Let $a,b,c,d$ be integers such that $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(c,d)=1$ and $ad-bc=k>0$. Prove that there are exactly $k$ pairs $(x_1,x_2)$ of rational numbers with $0\leq x_1,x_2<1$ for which both $ax_1+bx_2$ and $cx_1+dx_2$ are integers.

In the plane there are $5$ points $A, B, C, D, O$. Of these, $A, B, C, D$ lie on one line in this order, and $O$ is not on this line. If $OA = 16$, $OB = 10$, $OC = 9$, $OD = 12$ and $\angle AOB = \angle COD$, find the value of $\dfrac{BC}{AD}$. Here $XY$ denotes the length of the segment $XY$.

Initially all cells of a magical $5000\times70$ grid are grey. A painter stands on some cell and paints it red. Each second the painter takes two steps, one cell to the left and one cell down, and paints red the cell reached after both steps. A leftward step from the leftmost column takes the painter to the rightmost cell of the same row; a downward step from the bottom row takes the painter to the topmost cell of the same column. After some moves the painter returns to the starting cell. How many cells are red at that moment?

An ant walks from the bottom left corner of a $10\times 10$ square grid to the diagonally-opposite corner, always walking along grid lines and taking as short a route as possible. Let $N(k)$ be the number of different paths that ant could follow if it makes exactly $k$ turns. Find $N(6)-N(5)$.
A set $S$ of real numbers contains $1+1/x$ whenever it contains $x$. Can $S$ have exactly $2025$ elements?

Let $k$ be a positive integer. Lexi has a dictionary $\mathbb{D}$ consisting of some $k$-letter strings containing only the letters $A$ and $B$. Lexi would like to write either the letter $A$ or the letter $B$ in each cell of a $k\times k$ grid so that each column contains a string from $\mathbb{D}$ when read from top-to-bottom and each row contains a string from $\mathbb{D}$ when read from left-to-right.
What is the smallest integer $m$ such that if $\mathbb{D}$ contains at least $m$ different strings, then Lexi can fill her grid in this manner, no matter what strings are in $\mathbb{D}$?

Positive integers $a$ and $N$ are fixed, and $N$ positive integers are written on a blackboard. Alice and Bob play the following game. On Alice's turn, she must replace some integer $n$ on the board with $n+a$, and on Bob's turn he must replace some even integer $n$ on the board with $n/2$. Alice goes first and they alternate turns. If on his turn Bob has no valid moves, the game ends.

After analyzing the $N$ integers on the board, Bob realizes that, regardless of what moves Alice makes, he will be able to force the game to end eventually. Show that, in fact, for this value of $a$ and these $N$ integers on the board, the game is guaranteed to end regardless of Alice's or Bob's moves.

(a) The equation $uv + 3u - 3v - 18 = 0$ is equivalent to $(u - a)(v + b) = 9$. Write down the values of $a$ and $b$.
(b) Hence find all integer solutions of the equation $uv + 3u - 3v - 18 = 0$.
(Note: 'integers' means whole numbers, which can be positive, negative or zero.)
(c) Find all integer solutions of the equation $x^2 - y^2 + 6y - 18 = 0$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers.
Let $z_{1}$, $z_{2}$, $z_{3}$ be complex numbers such that $|z_{k}|=1$ $(k=1,2,3)$ $~$ and $~$ $\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}+\frac{z_{2}}{z_{3}}+\frac{z_{3}}{z_{1}}=1$ Find $|az_{1}+bz_{2}+cz_{3}|$.

Through a point $K$ of a circle, a chord $KA$ (the arc $KA$ being greater than $90^\circ$) and a tangent $l$ are drawn. The line through the centre $O$ of the circle perpendicular to the radius $OA$ meets the chord $KA$ at the point $B$ and the tangent $l$ at the point $C$. Prove that the segments $KC$ and $BC$ have the same length.

Acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with circumcircle $\omega$ is given. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$, $E$ be the foot of altitude from $A$ to $BC$, and $F$ be the intersection point of $AB$ and $DE$. Point $H$ lies on the arc $BC$ of $\omega$ (the one that does not contain $A$) such that $\angle BHE=\angle ABC$. Prove that $\angle BHF=90^\circ$.
A triangle $ABC$ and an interior point $P$ are given such that $AP = BC$, $\angle PBC = \angle PCB$ and $\angle PAC = \angle PCA = 20^\circ$. Compute the angles of the triangle $ABC$.

Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle ABC$, where $\angle BAC=120^{\circ}$. The tangent at $A$ to $(ABC)$ meets the tangents at $B,C$ at $(ABC)$ at points $P,Q$ respectively. Let $H,I$ be the orthocenter and incenter of $\triangle OPQ$ respectively. Define $M,N$ as the midpoints of arc $\overset{\frown}{BAC}$ and $OI$ respectively, and let $MN$ meet $(ABC)$ again at $D$. Prove that $AD$ is perpendicular to $HI$.

The cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper are coloured black and white in a chessboard pattern. Let $X$ be a triangle of area $S$ with vertices at grid nodes. Show that there is a triangle similar to $X$ with vertices at grid nodes such that the area of its white part equals the area of its black part and equals $S$.

Let $n$ and $a \leq n$ be two positive integers. There's $2n$ people sitting around a circle reqularly. Two people are friend iff one of their distance in the circle is $a$ (that is , $a-1$ people are between them). Find all integers $a$ in terms of $n$ st we can choose $n$ of these people , no two of them positioned in front of each other(means they're not antipodes of each other in the circle) and the total friendship between them is an odd number.
The number of faces of a pyramid multiplied by its number of edges is $5100$. Find the number of faces.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a cyclic hexagon such that $AD \parallel EF$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are marked on diagonals $AE$ and $DF$, respectively, such that $CX = EX$ and $BY = FY$. Let $O$ be the intersection point of $AE$ and $FD$, $P$ the intersection point of $CX$ and $BY$, and $Q$ the intersection point of $BF$ and $CE$. Prove that points $O$, $P$, and $Q$ are collinear.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. First, A writes pairwise distinct integers between $1$ and $n^2$ inclusive, one in each cell of an $n \times n$ grid. Next, B chooses some cells, no $2$ of which share a side (are adjacent), and the sum of the integers written in those cells is B's score. Find the largest possible integer $M$ such that, however A writes the numbers, B can always make the score at least $M$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The circle with center $A$ passing through $I$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $M$ and $N$. Prove that the line $MN$ is tangent to the incircle of triangle $ABC$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, its diagonals intersect at $E$. Let $H$, $G$ be the midpoints of its sides $AD$, $BC$ respectively. The circumscribed circles $c_1$ and $c_2$ of triangles $AEB$ and $DEC$ respectively intersect at point $F \ne E$. If the line passing through $E$ parallel to line $HG$ intersects circle $c_2$ at point $S$, prove that $FS \parallel CD$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with altitudes $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ meeting at $H$. The circle passing through points $D$, $E$, and $F$ meets $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ again at $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ respectively. Prove the following inequality: $$\frac{AH}{DX} + \frac{BH}{EY} + \frac{CH}{FZ} \ge 3.$$
Find all quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of positive real numbers such that $abcd=1$, $a^{2012}+2012b=2012c+d^{2012}$ and $2012a+b^{2012}=c^{2012}+2012d$.

Given a positive integer $k$, show that there exists a prime $p$ such that one can choose distinct integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{k+3} \in \{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}$ such that $p$ divides $a_ia_{i+1}a_{i+2}a_{i+3} - i$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k$.

After the end of an olympiad, the participants created three groups on Facebook. It is known that every participant joined exactly one group. For any two participants who are members of different groups, there are exactly $100$ members of the third group with whom both of these participants are friends, and there are also exactly $100$ members of the third group with whom neither of these two participants is friends (friendship is mutual). How many students took part in the olympiad in total?
There are $121$ points in the interior of a square of side $60$. Prove that three of them are the vertices of a triangle whose area is at most $30$.

The mayor of a city likes beautiful license plate numbers. In his opinion, a number is beautiful if, by inserting the symbols $+$, $-$, $\times$, $/$ and parentheses between and around its digits, one can obtain an expression whose value is divisible by $10$. To the mayor's delight, a reform of license plate numbers is planned in the city this month. What is the smallest number of digits that a license plate number must contain to guarantee that every car in the city has a beautiful license plate number? All license plate numbers in the city consist only of digits.

In a triangle $ABC,$ the internal and external bisectors of the angle $A$ intersect the line $BC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively. The line $AC$ meets the circle with diameter $DE$ again at $F.$ The tangent line to the circle $ABF$ at $A$ meets the circle with diameter $DE$ again at $G.$ Show that $AF = AG.$

Numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are given, each of which has exactly 2026 non-zero digits after the decimal point. Denote by $x_{(n)}$ the rounding of the number $x$, according to the rounding rules, to the $n$-th digit after the decimal point, for $n=1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2026$. Can it happen that:

a) $a_{(1)}+b_{(1)}>c_{(1)}+d_{(1)}$, $a_{(2)}+b_{(2)}<c_{(2)}+d_{(2)}$ and $a_{(3)}+b_{(3)}>c_{(3)}+d_{(3)}$?

b) for even $n$ the inequality $a_{(n)}+b_{(n)}<c_{(n)}+d_{(n)}$ holds, and for odd $n$ the inequality $a_{(n)}+b_{(n)}>c_{(n)}+d_{(n)}$ holds?

A teacher wants her $N$ students to know each other, so she creates various clubs of three people, each student being allowed to participate in several clubs. The clubs are formed in such a way that for any two people $A$ and $B$ there is exactly one club having both $A$ and $B$ among its three members.
(1) Show that there is no way for the teacher to form the clubs if $N = 11$.
(2) Show that the teacher can do it if $N = 9$.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be the midpoints of the diagonals $BD$ and $AC$ of the quadrilateral $ABCD$. Consider the points $M \in (BC)$, $N \in (CD)$, $R \in (PQ)$ and $S \in (AC)$ such that
$$\frac{BM}{MC} = \frac{DN}{NC} = \frac{PR}{RQ} = \frac{AS}{SC} = k.$$
Prove that the centroid of triangle $AMN$ lies on the segment $[RS]$.

An arithmetic progression is an infinite sequence $a_n=a_0+nd$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$, where $a_0,d$ are constants. A geometric progression is an infinite sequence $b_n=b_0q^n$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$, where $b_0,q$ are constants. (a) Does every arithmetic progression of integers contain an infinite subsequence that is a geometric progression? (b) Does every arithmetic progression of real numbers contain such an infinite subsequence?

Consider the tetrahedron $ABCD$ in which $G_1$, $G_2$, $G_3$ are the centroids of the faces $ADC$, $ABD$ and $BDC$, respectively.

a) Prove that the lines $BG_1$, $CG_2$, $AG_3$ are concurrent.

b) Knowing that $AG_3 = 8$, $BG_1 = 12$ and $CG_2 = 20$, compute the maximum possible value of the volume of the tetrahedron $ABCD$.

There are $2008$ trees arranged in a circle, with $1500$ ravens initially perched on distinct trees. On each move every raven flies to one of the two neighbouring trees. Is it possible that after finitely many moves all ravens are on the same tree?

The bisectors of the interior angles at the vertices $B$ and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $I$ and meet the sides $CA$ and $AB$ at the points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the segments $BI$ and $CI$, respectively. The line $FM$ meets the bisector of the exterior angle at vertex $B$ at the point $K$, and the line $EN$ meets the bisector of the exterior angle at vertex $C$ at the point $L$. Prove that the points $K, B, C, L$ lie on a circle.

Let $M$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2006\}$ with the following property: For any three elements $x$, $y$ and $z$ ($x < y < z$) of $M$, $x + y$ does not divide $z$. Determine the largest possible size of $M$. Justify your claim.

Let $AB$ be a chord, not a diameter, of a circle with center $O$. The smallest arc $AB$ is divided into three congruent arcs $AC$, $CD$, $DB$. The chord $AB$ is also divided into three equal segments $AC'$, $C'D'$, $D'B$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the lines $CC'$ and $DD'$. Prove that $\angle APB = \frac13 \angle AOB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. A circle $O$ passing through $B$ and $C$ meets the segments $AB$, $AC$ (endpoints excluded) at the points $D$, $E$ respectively, and $AD + AE = BC$ holds. Let $I$ be the incentre of triangle $ABC$, and let $P$, $Q$ be the points other than $B$, $C$ where the lines $BI$, $CI$ respectively meet the circle $O$. Prove that $A, I, P, Q$ lie on one circle.
Here $XY$ denotes the length of the segment $XY$.
Define $a_1=2$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n^3-a_n^2+1$ for $n\ge1$. Prove that any two distinct terms of the sequence are relatively prime.

A function $f$ on the nonnegative integers satisfies: (i) $f(n)$ is an integer for every $n$; (ii) $f(0)=1$; (iii) $$f(n+1)>f(n)+f(n-1)+\cdots+f(0)$$ for every $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. Determine the smallest possible value of $f(2023)$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle all of whose angles are acute, $\omega$ its circumcircle, and $O$ the centre of $\omega$. The altitude of $ABC$ from $A$ meets $\omega$ again at a point $D$ distinct from $A$, and the segment $[AC]$ meets the circumcircle of $OCD$ again at a point $E$ distinct from $C$. Finally, let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $[BE]$. Prove that $(DE)$ is parallel to $(OM)$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $\frac{a^4-1}{b+1}+\frac{b^4-1}{a+1}$ is an integer. Prove that $a^{2010}b^{2012}-1$ is divisible by $a+1$.

There are $n$ guests at a gathering. Any two are either friends or not friends. Every guest is friends with exactly four others. Whenever a guest is not friends with two other guests, those two cannot be friends with each other. Determine all possible values of $n$.
For any positive numbers $u, v$ prove the inequality $$\min\left\{u, \frac{100}{v}, v + \frac{2023}{u}\right\} \le \sqrt{2123}.$$ Here $\min X$ denotes the smallest element of the set $X$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral. Let $P$ be the intersection of the lines $BC$ and $AD$. Line $AC$ cuts the circumscribed circle of the triangle $BDP$ in $S$ and $T$, with $S$ between $A$ and $C$. The line $BD$ intersects the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ACP$ in $U$ and $V$, with $U$ between $B$ and $D$. Prove that $PS = PT = PU = PV$.

The positive integers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy both of the following equations.
$$\begin{cases} a + b = cd \\ c + d = ab \end{cases}$$
How many such quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ are there?

Consider real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2n}$ whose sum is $0$. Prove that among the pairs $(a_i, a_j)$, $i < j$, with $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 2n\}$, there exist at least $2n - 1$ pairs such that $a_i + a_j \geq 0$.

Eight different symbols are designed on $n\geq 2$ different T-shirts. Each shirt contains at least one symbol, and no two shirts contain exactly the same symbols. Suppose that for any $k$ symbols $(1\leq k\leq 7)$ the number of shirts containing at least one of the $k$ symbols is even. Determine the value of $n$.

Let $k$ be the circumcircle of a square $ABCD$. Let $P$ be a point on the shorter arc $CD$ of $k$ with $P \neq C$ and $P \neq D$. Let the intersection of the line $BP$ with the line $AC$ be $Q$, and let the intersection of the line $CP$ with the line $AD$ be $R$.

Prove that the line $RQ$ is perpendicular to the line $AC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$ and $C$ to the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $H$ the intersection point of the altitudes of $ABC$, and define $P$ to be the intersection of the segment $EF$ with the line $HD$. Let $M$ be a point on $AB$ and $N$ a point on $AC$ such that $MN$ is the line parallel to $BC$ that contains $P$. Show that $AMHN$ is cyclic.

Consider the natural number $n \ge 2$ and the real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in (0, \infty)$ with the property that there exists a nonzero natural number $k$ such that
$$a_1^{k-1} + a_2^{k} + \dots + a_n^{k+n-2} \ge a_1^{k} + a_2^{k+1} + \dots + a_n^{k+n-1}.$$
Prove that $a_1^k + a_2^k + \dots + a_n^k \le n$.

Let $A$ be a point outside a circle $\omega$. Two lines through $A$ meet $\omega$, the first at $B$ and $C$, the second at $D$ and $E$ ($D$ between $A$ and $E$). The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets $\omega$ again at $F$, and the line $AF$ meets $\omega$ again at $T$. Let $M$ be the intersection of the lines $BC$ and $ET$, $N$ the reflection of $A$ in $M$, and $K$ the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that the quadrilateral $DEKN$ is cyclic.
Find all pairs of coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the fraction $a/b$ is written in the decimal system as $b.a$.

Prove that
$$x^2 + \frac{8}{xy} + y^2 \ge 8$$
for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Solve the pair of simultaneous equations
$$x^2 - 2xy = 1,$$
$$5x^2 - 2xy + 2y^2 = 5.$$

Let $f$ be an increasing mapping from the family of subsets of a given finite set $H$ into itself, i.e. such that for every $X \subseteq Y \subseteq H$ we have $f(X) \subseteq f(Y) \subseteq H$. Prove that there exists a subset $H_0$ of $H$ such that $f(H_0) = H_0$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, $D$ is a point on segment $BC$. Let $R$ and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. The line $DR$ and the circumcircle of $BDS$ meet at $X$, with $X \ne D$. Similarly, the line $DS$ and the circumcircle of $CDR$ meet at $Y$, with $Y \ne D$. Prove that if $XY$ is parallel to $RS$, then $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $n>3$ be an integer and choose $a_k\in\{k,-k\}$ for $1\le k\le n$. Prove that there are indices $k_1,\ldots,k_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, not necessarily distinct, whose partial sums $\sum_{i=1}^j a_{k_i}$, $1\le j\le n$, have pairwise distinct residues modulo $2n+1$, with the last sum divisible by $2n+1$.

Some boys and girls are standing in a row, in some order, about to be photographed. All of them are facing the photographer. Each girl counts the number of boys to her left, and each boy counts the number of girls to his right.
Let the sum of the numbers counted by the girls be $G$, and the sum of the numbers counted by the boys be $B$.
Prove that $G = B$.

Let $r(x)$ be a polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients. Prove that there exist only finitely many pairs of polynomials $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ with real coefficients satisfying the equation $(p(x))^3+q(x^2)=r(x)$.

Determine all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers satisfying
$$x \mid (y + 1), \quad y \mid (z + 1) \quad \text{and} \quad z \mid (x + 1).$$
Let $P(x)=x^3+ax+b$, where $a,b$ are integers. Suppose that there are integers $y,z$ for which $P(y)-P(z)$ is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$. Prove that $a$ is not divisible by $3$.
A graph on $10^{100}$ vertices has no simple odd cycle of length at most $100$. Prove that it contains an independent set of size at least $10^{100}/102$.
Find all integer values of $n$, $0 \leq n \leq 2025$, $n \neq 3$, for which $\frac{1}{n^2 - 9}$ can be written as a terminating decimal.
If $n\in\mathbb{N}$, solve the equation $\cos^n x-\sin^n x=1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
Consider right triangles with integer side lengths whose hypotenuse has a length consecutive to that of one of the legs. How many such triangles exist?

Show that the set
$$A=\{\pm 1\pm 2\pm 3\pm\cdots\pm 2006\}$$
contains an even number of elements.

A triangular playground has sides, in metres, measuring $7$, $24$ and $25$. Inside the playground, a lawn is designed so that the distance from each point on the edge of the lawn to the nearest side is $2$ metres. What is the area of the lawn?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with a right angle at $A$ and $AB>AC$. The tangent at $A$ to the circumcircle $G$ of $ABC$ cuts $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ be the reflection of $A$ in the line $BC$, $X$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BE$, $Y$ the midpoint of $AX$, $Z$ the second intersection of $BY$ with $G$, and $F$ the intersection of $AE$ and $BC$. Prove that $D, Z, F, E$ are concyclic.

Consider the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ defined by $a_1 = 2024^{2024}$ and for each positive integer $n$,
$$a_{n+1} = \left|a_n - \sqrt{2}\right|.$$
Prove that there exists an integer $k$ such that $a_{k+2} = a_k$.

Here $|x|$ denotes the absolute value of $x$.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. Points $O_1$, $O_2$ lie on the sides $AB$, $AC$ respectively. It is known that the circle centered at $O_1$ and passing through $B$ is externally tangent to the circle centered at $O_2$ and passing through $C$ at a point $P$ inside the triangle. Find the angle $\angle BPC$.
How many numbers between $1$ and $1\,000$ are divisible by $3$ but have none of their digits divisible by $3$?

Let $(a_n)_{n\geq1}$ be an increasing sequence of positive integers such that $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}\leq2n$ for every positive integer $n$. Prove that every positive integer $n$ can be written as $n=a_p-a_q$ for some positive integers $p,q$.

A sequence of positive integers $a_n$ is defined as follows: $$a_0=3,\qquad a_{n+1}=(n+1)a_n-n\quad\text{for } n\ge 0.$$ Determine all positive integers $m$ such that $\gcd(m,a_n)=1$ for all $n\ge 0$.
Let $ABC$ be a non-isosceles triangle, and let $O,I,H$ be its circumcenter, incenter and orthocenter, respectively. Prove that $\angle OIH$ is obtuse.

Let $B,C,G,H$ lie on a circle with centre $A$ and radius $R$. Point $G$ lies on the extension of the median of triangle $ABC$ from $B$, and $H$ lies on the extension of its altitude from $B$. Let $X=AC\cap GH$. Prove that $AX=2R$.

Let $a,b,c$ be distinct positive real numbers with $\frac1{1+a}+\frac1{1+b}+\frac1{1+c}\le1$. Prove that $$2\left(\sqrt{\frac{a+b}{ac}}+\sqrt{\frac{b+c}{ba}}+\sqrt{\frac{c+a}{cb}}\right)<\frac{a^3}{(a-b)(a-c)}+\frac{b^3}{(b-c)(b-a)}+\frac{c^3}{(c-a)(c-b)}.$$

Michael is trying to move a counter around the cells of a $6\times 6$ grid according to the following rules:
• The counter can initially occupy any cell.
• Thereafter the counter moves alternately to a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell or jumps one cell horizontally or vertically.
• The first move is to an adjacent cell.
• The counter may never occupy the same cell twice.
His objective is for the counter to occupy every cell on the board at some point. Show him how to do it, or convince him he should stop trying.

Let $d\ge1$, $n\ge0$ be integers. Find the number of ways to put a non-negative integer in each square of a $d\times d$ grid so that the numbers in every set of $d$ squares, no two in the same row or column, sum to $n$.

junior.t:
Tom has twelve slips of paper which he wants to put into five cups labeled $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$. He wants the sum of the numbers on the slips in each cup to be an integer. Furthermore, he wants the five integers to be consecutive and increasing from $A$ to $E$. The numbers on the papers are $2, 2, 2, 2.5, 2.5, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3.5, 4,$ and $4.5$. If a slip with $2$ goes into cup $E$ and a slip with $3$ goes into cup $B$, then the slip with $3.5$ must go into what cup?

(A) $A$
(B) $B$
(C) $C$
(D) $D$
(E) $E$

Ana, Beatriz, Carlos, Diego and Emilia play a chess tournament.
Each player plays exactly once against each of the other four.
Each player scores $2$ points for winning a game, $1$ point for a draw and $0$ points for a loss.
At the end of the tournament it turns out that the scores of the $5$ players are all different.
Find the maximum number of draws there could have been in the tournament, and justify why there could not have been a larger number of draws.

Points $D$, $E$, $F$ lie on the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$, respectively, in such a way that $FB=BD$, $DC=CE$, and the lines $EF$ and $BC$ are parallel. The tangent to the circle circumscribed about the triangle $DEF$ at the point $F$ meets the segment $AD$ at a point $P$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $EF$ meets the segment $AC$ at a point $Q$. Prove that the lines $PQ$ and $BC$ are parallel.

Meta collects photos of famous sportsmen. Each year the number of her photos equals the sum of the numbers of her photos of the previous two years. In 2008 she had 60 photos and this year she has 96 photos. How many photos did she have in 2006?

(A) 20
(B) 24
(C) 36
(D) 40
(E) 48

In the plane, circles $k$ and $l$ are given which intersect at points $C$ and $D$, where the circle $k$ passes through the centre $L$ of the circle $l$. A line passing through the point $D$ meets the circles $k$ and $l$ for the second time at points $A$ and $B$, respectively, in such a way that $D$ is an interior point of the segment $AB$. Prove that $AB=AC$.

Bill walks $\tfrac12$ mile south, then $\tfrac34$ mile east, and finally $\tfrac12$ mile south. How many miles is he, in a direct line, from his starting point?

(A) $1$
(B) $1\tfrac14$
(C) $1\tfrac12$
(D) $1\tfrac34$
(E) $2$

How many subsets containing three different numbers can be selected from the set

$$\{ 89,95,99,132, 166,173 \}$$

so that the sum of the three numbers is even?

(A) $6$
(B) $8$
(C) $10$
(D) $12$
(E) $24$
In a certain triangle the measures of the interior angles are $a^\circ$, $b^\circ$, $c^\circ$, where $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Prove that this triangle is acute.

In my office, there are two clocks. One clock gains one minute every hour and the other loses two minutes every hour. Yesterday I set them both to the correct time but when I looked at them today, I saw that the time shown on one was 11:00 and shown on the other was 12:00. What time was it when I set the two clocks?

(A) 23:00
(B) 19:40
(C) 15:40
(D) 14:00
(E) 11:20

Each face of a regular tetrahedron with edge $2011$ is divided into $2011^2$ equilateral triangles of side $1$ by lines parallel to its sides. The players Bruno and Mariano mark triangles of side $1$, taking turns, one triangle each time; Bruno starts. Each marked triangle, except the first, must have at least one point in common with the triangle the opponent marked on his previous move. No triangle may be marked more than once. The player who cannot make a move loses. Determine which of the two players has a winning strategy and describe this strategy.
Take all four-digit numbers in which each of the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 occurs exactly once. What is the average of all these numbers?

Decide whether there exists a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ in whose interior one can find a point $P$ satisfying the conditions $$AB=AP,\quad BC=BP,\quad CD=CP,\quad DA=DP.$$

Note: A polygon is called convex if all of its interior angles have measure less than $180^\circ$.

Lucas paints the entire outside of a cube blue. He then saws the cube into 27 equally sized cubes. He neatly stacks these 27 cubes so that he gets a tower of $27\times 1\times 1$ cubes.
At most how many of the 110 side faces of cubes on the outside of his tower are blue?

There are $10$ playing cards and on each of them a different digit from $0$ to $9$ is written. Ana and Beto, taking turns, choose a card and place it to the right of the cards they have already placed previously, so that at the end of the game each player forms a $5$-digit number. Each player is forbidden to choose the $0$ on his first turn. Ana wins if her $5$-digit number is divisible by $6$. Otherwise Beto wins. Each player plays to win. If Ana plays first, determine which player has a winning strategy and explain his strategy.
The sum of the numbers $1$ to $123$ is $7626$. One number is omitted so that the sum is now a multiple of $4$. How many different numbers could be omitted?

The three sides of a triangle have consecutive integers as lengths. The length of the shortest side is $30\%$ of the perimeter of the triangle.
How long is the longest side?

Let $N$ be the smallest positive integer whose digits add up to $2015$.
What is the sum of the digits of $N + 1$?

Nicolas is planning to send a package to his friend Anton, who is a stamp collector. To pay for the postage, Nicolas would like to cover the package with a large number of stamps. Suppose he has a collection of $5$-cent, $10$-cent, and $25$-cent stamps, with exactly $20$ of each type. What is the greatest number of stamps Nicolas can use to make exactly $\$7.10$ in postage? (Note: The amount $\$7.10$ corresponds to $\$7$ and $10$ cents. One dollar is worth $100$ cents.)

(A) $45$
(B) $46$
(C) $51$
(D) $54$
(E) $55$

Let $c$ be a real number. If there are infinitely many triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying the system of equations
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3y + 9z &= 1 \\ x + 4y + 16z &= 1 \\ x + 5y + cz &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
which of the following can $c$ be?

(A) $19$
(B) $21$
(C) $23$
(D) $25$
(E) $27$

Rabbit Vasya loves cabbages and carrots. In a day, he eats either 9 carrots, or 2 cabbages, or 1 cabbage and 4 carrots. But some days he only eats grass. Over the last 10 days, Vasya ate a total of 30 carrots and 9 cabbages. On how many of these 10 days did he eat only grass?

(A) 0
(B) 1
(C) 2
(D) 3
(E) 4

Carrie has a rectangular garden that measures $6$ feet by $8$ feet. She plants the entire garden with strawberry plants. Carrie is able to plant $4$ strawberry plants per square foot, and she harvests an average of $10$ strawberries per plant. How many strawberries can she expect to harvest?

(A) $560$
(B) $960$
(C) $1120$
(D) $1920$
(E) $3840$
Assume that real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfy $$ab + \sqrt{ab + 1} + \sqrt{a^2 + b} \cdot \sqrt{b^2 + a} = 0.$$ Find, with proof, the value of $$a\sqrt{b^2 + a} + b\sqrt{a^2 + b}.$$

For real numbers $x, y$ satisfying the equation $(x^2 + y^2 - 25)(x + y) + 10xy = 0$, how many different integer values can the expression $x + y$ take?

(A) 2
(B) 4
(C) 6
(D) 10
(E) 12

A checkerboard consists of one-inch squares. A square card, $1.5$ inches on a side, is placed on the board so that it covers part or all of the area of each of $n$ squares. The maximum possible value of $n$ is

(A) $4$ or $5$
(B) $6$ or $7$
(C) $8$ or $9$
(D) $10$ or $11$
(E) $12$ or more

Let $ABC$ be a triangle in which $AB+AC=3\cdot BC$. Denote by $D$, $E$ the points such that the quadrilaterals $BCDA$ and $CBEA$ are parallelograms, and by $F$ and $G$ the points lying on the sides $AC$ and $AB$, respectively, such that $AF=AG=BC$. Prove that the intersection point of the lines $DF$ and $EG$ lies on the segment $BC$.

For $x=7$, which of the following is the smallest?

(A) $\dfrac{6}{x}$
(B) $\dfrac{6}{x+1}$
(C) $\dfrac{6}{x-1}$
(D) $\dfrac{x}{6}$
(E) $\dfrac{x+1}{6}$

Six standard, fair dice are rolled once. The total of the scores rolled is $32$.
What is the smallest possible score that could have appeared on any of the dice?

How many pairs $(x, y)$ of integers satisfy $2x^2 + 17xy + 35y^2 = 315$?

(A) 0
(B) 2
(C) 4
(D) 6
(E) 8
Show that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $a+b+c+abc=4$, $$\left(1+\frac{a}{b}+ca\right)\left(1+\frac{b}{c}+ab\right)\left(1+\frac{c}{a}+bc\right) \geq 27.$$

Two cyclists move with constant speeds on a circular track of length $800\,m$. When the cyclists move in opposite directions, they meet every $3$ minutes. But when they move in the same direction, the faster one overtakes the other every $24$ minutes. What is the speed of the faster cyclist in $km/h$?

(A) $7$
(B) $8$
(C) $9$
(D) $10$
(E) $11$

The circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect at the points $A$ and $B$. A line $\ell$ meets the circle $C_1$ at $C$ and $F$, the circle $C_2$ at $D$ and $G$, and the segment $[AB]$ at the point $E$. These points lie on the line $\ell$ in the order $C, D, E, F, G$. If $|CD| = 8$, $|DE| = 4$ and $|FG| = 6$, what is $|EF|$?

(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 4
(D) 5
(E) None

A circle is divided into $2n$ equal arcs by $2n$ points. Find all $n>1$ such that these points can be joined in pairs using $n$ segments, all of different lengths, so that each point is an endpoint of exactly one segment.

On a table there are several empty boxes, each of which can hold at most 2 balls. 19 balls can be placed into these boxes so that exactly 11 boxes remain empty, or 13 balls can be placed so that exactly 10 boxes remain empty. Then how many different values can the number of boxes on the table take?

(A) $1$
(B) $2$
(C) $3$
(D) $4$
(E) $5$

If the rational numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the equation $\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} = \sqrt{3 + \sqrt{5}}$, what is the sum of the distinct values the number $x$ can take?

(A) $3$
(B) $\dfrac{10}{3}$
(C) $4$
(D) $\dfrac{13}{4}$
(E) $\dfrac{8}{3}$

Farida makes a list of the integers between 1 and $10\,000$ that are divisible by 7. For every number on the list she adds the digits of the number.
What is the smallest number that occurs as an outcome?

(A) $1$
(B) $2$
(C) $3$
(D) $4$
(E) $5$

Fede painted each integer from $1$ to $100$ red or blue. There is at least one number of each colour. It is known that if two numbers have different colours and their sum is less than or equal to $100$, then the sum of the two numbers is red. Also, if two numbers have different colours and their product is less than or equal to $100$, then the product of the two numbers is blue. If $13$ is blue, determine all the numbers Fede painted blue.

There are 27 cardboard boxes and 27 plastic boxes, each containing coloured balls. No two boxes of the same type contain a ball of the same colour, but any two boxes of different types contain a ball of the same colour. In each step we choose two balls of the same colour in boxes of different types and paint them a colour of our choice. If, whatever the initial situation, we can make every box contain at least two balls of the same colour after at most $n$ steps, what is the smallest possible value of $n$?

A scalene triangle $ABC$ is given. It is known that $I$ is the center of the circle inscribed in this triangle, and the points $D$, $E$, $F$ are the points of tangency of this circle with the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$, respectively. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the lines $DE$ and $AI$. Prove that $CP \perp AI$.

A clock has the numbers 1 to 12 for indicating the hours. Ernie has interchanged these twelve numbers in such a way that any two adjacent numbers on the clock differ by either 2 or 3. Fortunately, the number 12 is still in the right place, but the 9 is where the 1 is supposed to be.
What number is in the place where the 9 is supposed to be?

Felix the Cat caught 12 fish in three days. Each day after the first he caught more fish than the previous day. On the third day he caught fewer fish than the first two days together. How many fish did Felix catch on the third day?

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 8
(E) 9
Is it possible to write $100$ odd numbers in a row in such a way that the sum of every $5$ adjacent numbers is a perfect square and the sum of every $9$ adjacent numbers is also a perfect square?

There are 10 ducks. 5 of these ducks lay an egg every day. The other 5 lay an egg every second day. How many eggs do the 10 ducks lay in a period of 10 days?

(A) 75
(B) 60
(C) 50
(D) 25
(E) 10

A palindrome is a number that has the same value when read from left to right or from right to left. (For example, 12321 is a palindrome.) Let $N$ be the least three-digit integer which is not a palindrome but which is the sum of three distinct two-digit palindromes. What is the sum of the digits of $N$?

(A) $2$
(B) $3$
(C) $4$
(D) $5$
(E) $6$

We call a 3-digit number nice if its middle digit is greater than the sum of its first and last digits. What is the largest possible number of consecutive nice 3-digit numbers?

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 8
(E) 9

Bartek patiently performs operations on fractions. In each move he adds to the current result its reciprocal, obtaining a new result. Bartek starts with the number $1$: after the first move he therefore obtains the result $2$, after the second move the result $\frac{5}{2}$, after the third $\frac{29}{10}$, etc. After $300$ moves Bartek obtained the result $x$. Determine the largest integer not greater than $x$.
Forty pipes are available; their lengths are $2$ m, $4$ m or $6$ m. There are as many $2$ m pipes as $6$ m pipes. What is the total length of the available pipes?

Every pupil in a class either swims or dances or both. Three fifths of the class swim and three fifths dance. Five pupils both swim and dance. How many pupils are there in the class?

(A) 15
(B) 20
(C) 25
(D) 30
(E) 35

Consider a square $ABCD$ with centre $O$. Let $E$, $F$, $G$ and $H$ be points in the interiors of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$, respectively, such that $AE = BF = CG = DH$. It is known that $OA$ meets $HE$ at the point $X$, $OB$ meets $EF$ at the point $Y$, $OC$ meets $FG$ at the point $Z$ and $OD$ meets $GH$ at the point $W$. Given that $\text{Area}(EFGH) = 1$, compute $$\text{Area}(ABCD)\times\text{Area}(XYZW).$$
How many pairs of (distinct) numbers taken from the set $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2002\}$ are there whose sum is an even number?

We say that a four-digit number $\overline{abcd}$ ($a \ne 0$) is porá if the following conditions hold:
$a \ge b$;
$\overline{ab} - \overline{cd} = \overline{cd} - \overline{ba}$.
For example, $2011$ is porá because $20 - 11 = 11 - 02$.
Find all the porá numbers.

Helga lives with her father, mother, brother and also one dog, two cats, two parrots and four goldfishes. How many legs do they have altogether?

(A) 22
(B) 28
(C) 24
(D) 32
(E) 13

In a certain group there are $n\geqslant 5$ people, where every two people who do not know each other have exactly one common acquaintance, and no person knows all the others. Prove that $5$ of the given $n$ people can be seated at a round table so that each of them sits between two of their

(a) acquaintances,

(b) non-acquaintances.

Véra and Blaise play the following game on a cube. Véra paints an edge green, then Blaise paints another edge blue. Then Véra paints green an edge not yet painted, then Blaise paints blue an edge not yet painted. They continue in this way until all the edges are painted. At the end, Véra counts the number of vertices that are an endpoint of at least one green edge. Véra wishes to maximise this number of vertices. Is the largest value of this number that Véra is sure to obtain by playing well:

(a) at least $6$?

(b) at least $7$?

(c) $8$?

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ about which a circle can be circumscribed is given. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides $AD$ and $CD$ are drawn; they intersect at the point $Q$ and meet the sides $BC$ and $AB$ at the points $P$ and $K$, respectively. It turned out that the points $K$, $B$, $P$, $Q$ lie on one circle. Prove that the points $A$, $Q$, $C$ lie on one line.

For a convex polygon (i.e. all angles less than $180^\circ$) call a diagonal bisector if it bisects both area and perimeter of the polygon. What is the maximum number of bisector diagonals for a convex pentagon?

In a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ABC=15^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=30^\circ$, let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. The line perpendicular to $BC$ passing through $A$ meets $BC$ at the point $D$. Compute the measure of the angle $\angle MAD$.

Given a set of ten positive integers, not necessarily distinct, the following ten operations are performed: the first one is discarded and the remaining nine are added; the second one is discarded and the remaining nine are added; and so on until the last one is discarded and the remaining nine are added. In this way only nine different results are obtained, namely $86, 87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 96$. Find the ten initial numbers.

Consider a rectangle $ABCD$ with center $O$ and $AB \neq BC$. The perpendicular dropped from $O$ to $BD$ intersects the lines $AB$ and $BC$ at $E$ and $F$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the segments $[CD]$ and $[AD]$. Prove that $FM \perp EN$.

Let $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ be a regular polygon with $n$ sides, $n\ge 3$. Initially there are three ants standing at the vertex $A_1$. Each minute two ants move simultaneously to a neighbouring vertex, but in different directions (one clockwise and the other counterclockwise), and the third stays at the vertex where it is. Determine all values of $n$ for which after some time the three ants can meet at the same vertex of the polygon, different from $A_1$.
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exist $n$ distinct positive rational numbers the sum of whose squares equals $n$.

Using the digits $0$, $1$ and $2$ a sequence is written in stages. In the first stage a $0$ is written, and from then on, at each stage as many digits are appended as there already were. To write the new digits, the digits already written are copied, but changing $0$ into $1$, $1$ into $2$ and $2$ into $0$. The following examples show the sequence after the first, second, third, fourth and fifth stage, respectively: $$0;\quad 01;\quad 0112;\quad 01121220;\quad 0112122012202001.$$ Determine which digit occupies position $1000000$ of the sequence.

Two runners are training on a 720 metre circular track. They run in opposite directions, each at constant speed. The first runner takes four minutes to complete the full loop and the second runner takes five minutes. How many metres does the second one run between two consecutive meetings of the two runners?

(A) 355
(B) 350
(C) 340
(D) 330
(E) 320
Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon such that $AB=BC=CD$ and $\angle BDE=\angle EAC=30^\circ$. Find the possible values of $\angle BEC$.

In a particular month there were 5 Saturdays and 5 Sundays, but only 4 Fridays and 4 Mondays. In the next month there were

(A) 5 Wednesdays
(B) 5 Thursdays
(C) 5 Fridays
(D) 5 Saturdays
(E) 5 Sundays
Is there a convex polyhedron which has an odd number of edges and each of whose faces has an even number of sides? Justify your answer.

Beto wrote $36$ consecutive positive integers on the blackboard. He computed the sum of all the digits of the $16$ smallest numbers and wrote the result in blue. Then he computed the sum of all the digits of the $10$ largest numbers and wrote the result in red. Is it possible that the blue number is less than or equal to the red number? If the answer is yes, show what the numbers Beto wrote can be; if the answer is no, explain why it is impossible.

During some month, 5 Mondays occurred. Then this month could not have

(A) 5 Saturdays
(B) 5 Sundays
(C) 5 Tuesdays
(D) 5 Wednesdays
(E) 5 Thursdays

We say that a positive integer $n$ is good if the result of multiplying the first $n$ odd positive integers uses only the digits $1$, $3$, $5$ and $9$. For example, $n = 3$ is good, because $1\cdot 3\cdot 5 = 15$, but $n = 4$ is not, because $1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7 = 105$.
Find all the good numbers.
A four-digit number, $n$, is written as '$ABCD$' where $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are all different odd digits. It is divisible by each of $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. Find all the possible numbers for $n$.
Find all triples of natural numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $x$ plus twice $y$ plus twice $z$ equals $x$ times $y$ times $z$, that is, $$x+2y+2z=xyz.$$

The following text is written on a blackboard:

The equation $x^2 - 824x + \blacksquare 143 = 0$ has two integer solutions.

Here $\blacksquare$ represents some number of digits of a number that have been smudged on the board. What are the possible equations originally on the board?

Alix, Bénédicte and Claude each have a square wooden board whose thickness is $1$ cm. The measures in centimetres of the sides of these boards are odd integers. These three boards are cut into small cubes of edge $1$ cm by saw cuts parallel to their sides. These cubes are then gathered into a single pile and the three friends use them to form as many cubes of edge $2$ cm as possible. When this work is finished, three small unit cubes remain unassembled. Explain why this was predictable.

On a table there are $n$ empty red boxes numbered $1,2,\ldots,n$ and $n$ empty white boxes numbered $1,2,\ldots,n$. In each move, one ball is placed in each of two boxes of different colours. After several moves, for every pair of a red and a white box with the same number, either the red box contains 6 more balls than the white box or the white box contains 16 more balls than the red box. Find all possible values of $n$.

It takes one minute for a train travelling at constant speed to pass completely through a tunnel that is $120$ metres long. The same train, travelling at the same constant speed, takes $20$ seconds from the instant its front enters the tunnel to it being completely inside the tunnel.
How long is the train?
Agnes wrote $2027$ pairwise distinct prime numbers around a circle. Is it possible that all $2027$ sums of pairs of adjacent primes on the circle are perfect squares?

A rhombus $ABCD$ is given in which $\angle ABC=100^\circ$. Point $P$ lies on side $CD$, and $\angle PBC=20^\circ$. The line parallel to side $AD$ passing through point $P$ meets the diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Prove that $BP=AQ$.

Jenny had to add 26 to a certain number. Instead she subtracted 26 and obtained $-14$. What number should she have obtained?

(A) 28
(B) 32
(C) 36
(D) 38
(E) 42

There are $100$ pairwise distinct positive real numbers written on the board, such that for any three distinct numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ among them the number $a^2+bc$ is an integer. Prove that for any two numbers $x$, $y$ from the board the number $\frac{x}{y}$ is rational.

When the real numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy $ab + bc + cd = 1$, find the smallest possible value of
$$(a^2 + ac + c^2)(b^2 + bd + d^2).$$
How many three-digit integers less than $1000$ have exactly two different digits in their representation (for example, $232$, or $466$)?
Determine all positive integers that cannot be written as $\dfrac ab+\dfrac{a+1}{b+1}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers.

A teacher gave each of her $37$ pupils $36$ crayons of different colours. It turned out that every pair of pupils received exactly one crayon of the same colour. Determine the smallest possible number of different colours of the distributed crayons.

Below, the notation $\overline{xy\ldots z}$ represents the number whose digits are, from left to right, $x$, $y$, $\ldots$ and $z$; in the case of three digits, therefore, $\overline{xyz} = 100x + 10y + z$.
Determine all three-digit numbers $\overline{abc}$ such that
$$\overline{abc} = \overline{ab} + \overline{bc} + \overline{ca} + \overline{ba} + \overline{cb} + \overline{ac}$$
(for example, $152$ is not such a number since $\overline{152} \neq \overline{15} + \overline{52} + \overline{21} + \overline{51} + \overline{25} + \overline{12}$).

Which number when squared is increased by 500%?

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 8
(E) 10

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point in its interior such that $\angle DBC = 60^\circ$ and $\angle DCB = \angle DAB = 30^\circ$. If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$, respectively, prove that $\angle DMN = 90^\circ$.

An employee at the supermarket is stacking crisps canisters. There are two types of canisters: small ones and large ones. Three small canisters stack to the same height as one large canister. The employee makes a stack of 12 small canisters. Next to it, he makes more stacks of the same height, but all stacks are different. (If one stack starts with a small canister followed by a large one, and the other starts with a large one followed by a small one, the two stacks are different.)
How many different stacks can he make, including the first stack?

The masses of salt and fresh water in sea water in Protaras are in the ratio $7:193$. How many kilograms of salt are there in 1000 kg of sea water?

(A) 35
(B) 186
(C) 193
(D) 200
(E) 350

Schoolmates Andy, Betty, Cathie and Dannie were born in the same year. Their birthdays were on February 20th, April 12th, May 12th and May 25th, not necessarily in this order. Betty and Andy were born in the same month. Andy and Cathie were born in the same day of different months. Who of these schoolmates is the oldest?

(A) Andy
(B) Betty
(C) Cathie
(D) Dannie
(E) impossible to determine

Four brothers have eaten 11 cookies in total. Each of them has eaten at least one cookie and no two of them have eaten the same number of cookies. Three of them have eaten 9 cookies in total and one of them has eaten exactly 3 cookies. How many cookies have been eaten by the boy who has eaten the largest number of cookies?

(A) 3
(B) 4
(C) 5
(D) 6
(E) 7

A fruit bowl contains five types of fruit: apples, grapes, cherries, strawberries and bananas.
Al likes apples.
Bok likes apples, cherries, strawberries and bananas.
Cam likes grapes, cherries, strawberries and bananas.
Don likes apples, grapes and cherries.
Eva likes apples and cherries.
The fruit is shared so that everyone gets a different type of fruit and everyone gets a type of fruit that they like. Who gets cherries?

(A) Al
(B) Bok
(C) Cam
(D) Don
(E) Eva

A triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ACB=90^\circ$ is given. Point $D$ is the foot of the altitude drawn from the vertex $C$, and points $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. The bisector of the angle $BAC$ meets the line $EF$ at a point $P$. Prove that the point $P$ is the centre of the circle inscribed in the triangle $CDE$.

A ladder has 21 stairs. Nick and Mike are counting stairs one – from bottom to top, another – from top to bottom. They met on a stair that was called the 10th by Nick. What number will Mike give to this stair?

(A) 13
(B) 14
(C) 11
(D) 12
(E) 10

Let $ABC$ be a right-angled triangle with $\angle BAC = 90^{\circ}$ and let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Let $Z \ne A$ be a point on the line $AB$ with $AB = BZ$. Let $(c)$ be the circumcircle of triangle $AEZ$. Let $D$ be the second point of intersection of $(c)$ with $ZC$ and let $F$ be the point of $(c)$ diametrically opposite to $D$. Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the lines $FE$ and $CZ$. If the tangent to $(c)$ at $Z$ meets $PA$ at $T$, prove that the points $T$, $E$, $B$, $Z$ are concyclic.

Liselotte has a collection of 100 candies, which are either sweet or bitter. She wants to choose between the following possibilities.
I) She eats half of the sweet candies. The rest is kept in the bag.
II) She eats half of the bitter candies. The rest is kept in the bag.
The part of the remaining candies in case I that are bitter, is three times as large as the part of remaining candies in case II that are bitter.
How many bitter candies does the bag contain (before Liselotte eats any of them)?

For any natural number $N$ with $2k$ digits, let $I(N)$ be the $k$-digit number obtained by writing the digits of odd order of $N$ from left to right, and $P(N)$ the $k$-digit number obtained by writing the digits of even order of $N$ from left to right. For example, $I(249035) = 405$ and $P(249035) = 293$. Prove that it is not possible to find a natural number $N$ with $2k$ digits such that $N = I(N)\cdot P(N)$.
Find all integers $n \ge 1$ such that $n \cdot 2^{n+1}+1$ is a perfect square.

Ema has to write a number and calculate the product of its digits. The result has to be greater than $2026$. Determine the smallest number Ema can write.
(For example, the product of the digits of the number $1234$ is $1 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24$.)

In a triangle $ABC$, $\angle C=45^\circ$, $Q$ is the foot of the altitude from vertex $B$ and $M$ is the midpoint of side $AB$. Let $P$ be on side $BC$ such that $PM$ is perpendicular to $QM$. Decide whether for some value of the angle $A$ one has $$\frac{PQ^2}{PM^2}=3.$$
Prove that every integer greater than $5$ can be written as the sum of a prime number and a composite number.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. Points $O_1$, $O_2$ lie on the sides $AB$, $AC$ respectively. It is known that the circle centered at $O_1$ and passing through $B$ is externally tangent to the circle centered at $O_2$ and passing through $C$ at a point $P$ inside the triangle. Find the angle $\angle BPC$.

Given is a triangle $ABC$ such that $|AC|=|BC|$, $|AB|=\sqrt{3}$ and $|CD|=\sqrt{2}$, where $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Let $E$ and $F$ denote the midpoints of sides $CB$ and $DB$, respectively, and let $G$ denote the point of intersection of lines $AE$ and $CF$. Prove that the point $D$ belongs to an angle bisector of angle $AGF$.

To defeat a dragon Mathias has to cut off all the dragon's heads. If he can cut off 3 dragon's heads, one new head immediately grows. Mathias defeats the dragon by cutting off 13 heads in total. How many heads did the dragon have at the beginning?

(A) 8
(B) 9
(C) 10
(D) 11
(E) 12
If $x$, $y$ and $z$ are non-zero and pairwise distinct real numbers such that $$\frac{x^2-yz}{x(1-yz)}=\frac{y^2-xz}{y(1-xz)}$$ prove that $$x+y+z=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}.$$

The number 100 is multiplied either by 2 or by 3, then the result is increased either by 1 or by 2, and then the new result is divided either by 3 or by 4. The final result is a natural number. What is this final result?

(A) 50
(B) 51
(C) 67
(D) 68
(E) There is more than one possible final result.
Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geq 3$. Find all $n$ for which there exists an $n$-gon all of whose interior angles are $120^\circ$ or $240^\circ$ and all of whose sides have equal length.

The letters $a$, $b$ and $c$ stand for non-zero digits. The integer '$abc$' is a multiple of $3$; the integer '$cbabc$' is a multiple of $15$; and the integer '$abcba$' is a multiple of $8$.
What is the integer '$abc$'?
Is it possible to find two distinct powers of $2$, with the same number of digits, such that one of them can be obtained by reordering the digits of the other?

How many common letters do the words KANGAROO and PROBLEM have?

(A) 5
(B) 1
(C) 7
(D) 2
(E) 3

$n$ is a positive integer each of whose digits is between $1$ and $7$ inclusive. $n$ is a multiple of $7$, and moreover, however the digits of $n$ are rearranged, the result is again a multiple of $7$. Find all possible such $n$.

A circle is circumscribed about an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$. The bisector of angle $C$ and the bisector of angle $A$ meet the circle at the points $E$ and $D$, respectively, and the segment $DE$ meets the sides $BC$ and $AB$ at the points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Reconstruct $\triangle ABC$ from the points $D$, $P$, $Q$, if it is known in which half-plane with respect to the line $DQ$ the vertex $A$ lies.

There are black discs and white discs distributed in $3$ piles. In each pile the colours alternate as follows, counting from the bottom: $11$ black, $10$ white, $9$ black, $8$ white, $\ldots$, $3$ black, $2$ white, $1$ black. A legal move is to remove one or several discs of the same colour from those on top of a pile, without rearranging the rest. Two players, Ana and Brian, make moves in turn until all the discs have been removed; Ana starts the game. Determine which player has a winning strategy if the one who removes the last disc loses.

$ABC$ is an acute triangle with $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$. A point $X$ is taken inside triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle XBC = \angle XCB = 30^\circ$. Points $P$, $Q$ are taken on the lines $BX$, $CX$ respectively so that $AP = BP$ and $AQ = CQ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that $\angle PMQ = 90^\circ$.
Here $YZ$ denotes the length of the segment $YZ$.
Consider the six-digit multiples of three with at least one of each of the digits $0$, $1$ and $2$, and no other digits. What is the difference between the largest and the smallest of these numbers?

Arash is given a paper isosceles right triangle. A folding of this paper is called good if the polygon obtained after this fold has all angles less than $180^\circ$. Arash performs a good fold. Babak takes the paper and performs two good folds, so that the paper is folded exactly three times at the end. Arash wants the final polygon to have the most possible number of sides but Babak wants the opposite. Assuming they do their best, how many sides does the final polygon have?

Find all pairs $(x,y)$ of positive integers such that
$$xy\mid x^2+2y-1.$$
Let $P$ be a convex pentagon with all sides equal. Prove that if two of the angles of $P$ add up to $180$ degrees, then it is possible to cover the plane with copies of $P$, without overlaps.

There are $390$ gold coins distributed in $30$ chests: $13$ coins in each chest. Each coin weighs an integer number of grams, greater than or equal to $1$ and less than or equal to $30$, and there are $13$ coins of each weight. It is known that if two coins are in the same chest, the difference between their weights is less than or equal to $4$ grams. Determine the minimum possible value of the weight of the contents of the heaviest chest.

The triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB=AC$ and $\angle BAC<60^{\circ}$. The points $D$ and $E$ are chosen on the side $AC$ such that $EB=ED$ and $\angle ABD=\angle CBE$. Denote by $O$ the intersection point of the internal bisectors of the angles $BDC$ and $ACB$. Compute $\angle COD$.

Find the number of pairs of two-digit natural numbers whose difference is equal to 50.

(A) 40
(B) 30
(C) 50
(D) 60
(E) 10

The angle $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ measures $120^\circ$. Let $M$ be a point on the side $AC$ and $K$ a point on the extension of the side $AB$ such that $BM$ is the internal bisector of the angle $\angle ABC$ and $CK$ is the external bisector corresponding to the angle $\angle ACB$. The segment $MK$ meets $BC$ at the point $P$. Prove that $\angle APM = 30^\circ$.
Prove that, for every positive integer $n$, there exist positive integers $a$ and $b$ with no common prime factors such that $a^2 + 2017b^2$ has more than $n$ distinct prime factors.

Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$. We say that $M$ is a medial point of the square if there exist two points $P$, $Q$ on the sides of the square such that $PQ=1$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$. Determine the set of all medial points of the square $ABCD$.

We call a pair of positive integers $(n,k)$ with $k>1$ a lovely couple if there exists an $n\times n$ table consisting of ones and zeros with the following properties:
• in every row there are exactly $k$ ones;
• for every two rows there is exactly one column such that at both intersections of that column with the mentioned rows the number one is written.
Solve the following subproblems:
a) Let $d\ne 1$ be a divisor of $n$. Determine all remainders that $d$ can give when divided by $6$.
b) Prove that there exist infinitely many lovely couples.
$ABCD$ is a trapezium whose base $DC$ is three times as long as the base $AB$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $AD$, what fraction of the area of the trapezium is the area of the triangle $BDM$?

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Morgane has coloured the integers $1, 2, \ldots, n$. Each of them is coloured in exactly one colour. It turned out that for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a<b$ and $a+b\le n$, at least two of the integers among $a$, $b$ and $a+b$ are of the same colour. Prove that there exists a colour that has been used for at least $2n/5$ integers.

Determine the smallest integer $n\geqslant 1$ with the property that an $n\times n$ square can be cut into square pieces of dimensions $1\times 1$ or $2\times 2$ in such a way that the same number of pieces of each of these two kinds is obtained.
Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are nonzero and satisfy the system of equations $$\begin{cases} a^2+a=b^2\\ b^2+b=c^2\\ c^2+c=a^2. \end{cases}$$ Prove that $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)=1$.

Five children, Achmed, Bob, Celine, Dirk and Eva, are standing in the queue for an ice-cream stand. They all have a whole number of euros with them to buy an ice cream.
